'''Shelby G. Tilford''' (January 11, 1937 – June 10, 2022)<ref>{{cite web | title=Shelby Tilford Obituary (1937 – 2022) - Washington, SC - The Washington Post | website=Legacy.com | date=June 14, 2022 | url=https://www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/washingtonpost/name/shelby-tilford-obituary?id=35204597 | access-date=June 19, 2022}}</ref> was an American atmospheric spectroscopist, Earth scientist, and science program administrator. He retired in 1994 after a long career with the [[National Aeronautics and Space Administration]], most recently serving as the Acting Associate Administrator of NASA's Office of [[Mission to Planet Earth]]. He is recognized as one of the main initiators of the Earth system science concept and NASA's Mission to Planet Earth program, which represented NASA's contribution to the [[U.S. Global Change Research Program]] (USGCRP).<ref name=asrar>{{cite book |last=Asrar |first=G. |date=1995 |title=Preface. In: The State of Earth Science from Space: Past Progress, Future Prospects (G. Asrar and D. Dokken, Eds) |publisher=American Institute of Physics}}</ref>

== Education ==
Tilford majored in chemistry, math and physics at [[Western Kentucky University]], and went on to graduate school at [[Vanderbilt University]] where he completed a PhD thesis on spectra of dinitrogen substituted benzene rings. He then moved to the [[Naval Research Laboratory]] (NRL) in [[Washington, DC]] where he conducted research on spectral lines of atmospheric molecules in the region above 1000 [[angstroms]].<ref name=history1>{{cite web |last=Wright |first=Rebecca |title=Earth System Science at 20 Oral History Project |date=23 June 2009 |url=https://historycollection.jsc.nasa.gov/JSCHistoryPortal/history/oral_histories/NASA_HQ/ESS/TilfordSG/TilfordSG_6-23-09.htm |publisher=NASA}}</ref>

== Career ==
In 1976 Tilford went to [[NASA Headquarters]] as a detailee in the [[Solar Physics]] program, which led to a position as head of NASA's newly established Upper Atmosphere Research Program (UARP). An important science issue for the UARP was to understand the nature and causes of atmospheric [[ozone depletion]] and the impact of [[chlorofluorocarbons]] (CFCs). After several years, [[Chlorofluorocarbon|CFC]]s were eventually banned on a global scale (see [[Montreal Protocol]]).
By late 1978, NASA had consolidated all its Earth science research observation components, including atmosphere, oceans, land, solar-terrestrial physics, and the aircraft observations  into an integrated Earth Science Division in the Office of Space Science, under Tilford's purview.<ref name=pecora>{{cite web |date=1992 |title=William T. Pecora Award |url=https://www.usgs.gov/media/files/shelby-g-tilford-citation |publisher=USGS}}</ref>

At UNISPACE '82 in [[Vienna]] (a conference of the [[United Nations Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space]]), Tilford and colleagues, in a NASA delegation led by Administrator [[James M. Beggs|James Beggs]], proposed a Global Habitability initiative as an international cooperative research effort to obtain data on the Earth's environment, hoping to obtain international support for the concept. However, it was not generally well received.<ref name=barton>{{cite web |last=Barton |first=Jenifer |date=2020 |title=Wiring the World: A History of the Earth System Concept in the US Earth Sciences, 1982-1989 |url=https://tspace.library.utoronto.ca/bitstream/1807/103621/1/Barton_Jenifer_Patricia_202011_PhD_thesis.pdf |page=92 |publisher=University of Toronto}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |date=March 1983 |title=UNISPACE '82: A Context for International Cooperation and Competition |url=https://govinfo.library.unt.edu/ota/Ota_4/DATA/1983/8328.PDF |pages=52–53}}</ref> Following this Tilford, with top agency officials formulated the Earth System Science Committee (ESSC) of the [[NASA Advisory Council]], chaired by [[Francis Bretherton]], to put together the foundation for a new comprehensive NASA initiative in Earth science from space.<ref name=history1/><ref name=barton/> After extensive deliberations amongst the scientific community a final report was released in 1988 (Earth System Science: A Closer View).<ref>{{cite book |last=National Research Council |date=1988 |title=Earth System Science: A Closer View | publisher=National Academies Press}}</ref> This set the stage for Tilford's development and leadership of NASA's [[Earth Observing System]] (EOS) and the associated data system, the [[EOSDIS|EOS Data and Information System (EOSDIS)]].<ref name="award">{{cite web |title=1993 Presidential Rank Awards |year = 1993|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=oKMrH688KzAC&q=shelby+tilford+nasa+presidential+rank+award&pg=PA20}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |date=7 May 1993 |title=Mission to Planet Earth May Be Vulnerable to NASA Budget Cuts |url=https://www.aip.org/fyi/1993/mission-planet-earth-may-be-vulnerable-nasa-budget-cuts |publisher=American Institute of Physics}}</ref> As preparation for EOS got underway, Tilford and counterparts in other U.S. agencies with responsibilities in Earth science created the [[U.S. Global Change Research Program]] (USGCRP).<ref name=pecora/><ref name=ncse>{{cite web |date=29 January 2014 |last=Institute for Global Environmental Strategies |title=Shelby Tilford To Receive NCSE Lifetime Achievement Award |url=https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/shelby-tilford-to-receive-ncse-lifetime-achievement-award-242583401.html |publisher=PRNewswire}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Dutton |first=J. |date=1995 |title=Scientific Priorities in Global Change Research. In: The State of Earth Science from Space: Past Progress, Future Prospects (G. Asrar and D. Dokken, Eds) |page=106 |publisher=American Institute of Physics}}</ref> The USGCRP was established by Presidential initiative in 1989.<ref name=ncse/> EOS subsequently received budgetary funding as a new start in 1990, and a new NASA Office of [[Mission to Planet Earth]] was created with Tilford as Acting Associate Administrator.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Asrar |first1=G. |last2=Tilford |first2=S. |last3=Butler |first3=D. |date=1992 |title=Mission to planet earth: Earth observing system |journal=Palaeogeography, Palaeoclimatology, Palaeoecology |volume=98 |issue=1 |pages=3–8|doi=10.1016/0031-0182(92)90251-Y |bibcode=1992PPP....98....3A }}</ref><ref name=watson>{{cite book |last=Watson |first=R. |date=1995 |title=Foreword. In: The State of Earth Science from Space: Past Progress, Future Prospects (G. Asrar and D. Dokken, Eds) |publisher=American Institute of Physics}}</ref>
